summary: Defines an XML format extension for representing copy control attributes in resource lists. When a SIP request is sent to a group of recipients through a server, the list of URIs is carried as a resource list XML document. The extension marks whether each recipient is addressed directly, copied, or blind-copied. It has been updated since.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5364 adds the to, cc and bcc labels to SIP resource lists, the lists of addresses that say who a request goes to. A server that fans the request out builds a new list for each recipient, keeping the visible names and hiding the blind ones.

questions: xml extension for to cc bcc in resource list
what is copycontrol in sip resource lists
how does sip support bcc recipients
subtitle: Lets a SIP sender mark each recipient as to, cc or bcc, the way an email sender can.

tldr.problem: When a SIP request is sent to a group through a server, the list of recipients travels as an XML resource list, but nothing in it says who is a main recipient, who is a copy and who is a blind copy.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a copyControl attribute with the values to, cc and bcc, plus an anonymize attribute and a count attribute. The server copies the visible recipients into a recipient-history list it sends to each recipient, and removes the blind copies.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Proposed Standard from October 2008 and was later updated by RFC 8996. A recipient that cannot see itself in the history list should not be allowed to reply to everyone, or the blind copy would be revealed.

today: RFC 5364 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2008. It was later updated by RFC 8996; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Copy Control for SIP Requests
sections.content:
RFC 5363 describes a generic framework for carrying Uniform Resource Identifier lists in SIP messages, providing a common framework for specific URI-list services such as conferences initiated with INVITE requests or multiple-recipient MESSAGE requests. Common to all of them is a SIP request that contains a collection of resources, typically expressed as an XML resource list. Such requests appear either in the requests received by the URI-list server, indicating the list of intended recipients, or in each of the requests the server sends to recipients, indicating the list of recipients of the same request.

Although the XML resource list provides a powerful mechanism for describing a list of resources, there is a need for a copy control attribute to determine whether a resource is receiving a SIP request as a primary recipient, a carbon copy or a blind carbon copy. This is similar to common email systems, where the sender can categorize each recipient as a "to", "cc" or "bcc" recipient. This document provides an extension to the XML resource list that lets the sender supply a copy control attribute labelling each recipient as a "to", "cc" or "bcc" recipient, and that indicates whether the recipient is receiving a primary copy, a carbon copy or a blind carbon copy. It also gives the sender the ability to mark resources as anonymized, so that some recipients' URIs are not disclosed to the others and are replaced with anonymous URIs instead.
sections.plainLanguage: Email lets you mark who is a main recipient, who gets a copy and who gets a hidden copy. SIP had no way to say this, so this document adds it to the list of addresses carried in a SIP request.

sections.title: How a URI-List Server Expands a Request
sections.content:
Figure 1 of the RFC shows the general operation of a URI-list server. A SIP User Agent Client issuer sends a SIP request, flow F1, to a URI-list server containing a recipient list. The server generates a SIP request to each recipient, according to the specific SIP method. Each of these requests contains a recipient-history list indicating the visible list of recipients of the request. The server replies to the issuer with a 2xx response, flow F2, and each recipient replies with a 200 OK, flows F6, F7 and F8.

The recipient list includes the target URIs of the request, and each target URI may also be marked with a copy control attribute to indicate the copy level in which the recipient is receiving the request. This is achieved by qualifying each URI with a 'copyControl' attribute whose values are "to", "cc" and "bcc". When the server expands the request, it includes a recipient-history resource list built upon the recipient list it received, and that list replaces the recipient list in the requests it generates. The server copies the targets marked "to" and "cc" into the recipient-history list and explicitly excludes the URIs marked "bcc", although it can preserve the address of a "bcc" tagged URI when it matches the URI of the recipient of the request.

When a recipient receives the request with the recipient-history list, it can determine which other visible recipients are getting a copy and whether they are marked "to" or "cc", and later, if needed, generate a reply to those visible recipients.
sections.plainLanguage: The server takes the sender's list, sends one copy of the request to each address, and puts a shortened list inside each copy so the recipients can see who else got it. Blind copies are left out of that list.

sections.title: The copyControl, anonymize and count Attributes
sections.content:
The copyControl attribute is added to the entry element of the resource list document format. It has similar semantics to the type of destination address in email systems and can take the values "to", "cc" and "bcc". A "to" value indicates that the resource is a primary recipient of the request, "cc" indicates that it receives a carbon copy, and "bcc" indicates that it receives a blind carbon copy, meaning the URI is not disclosed to the other recipients. The default copyControl value is "bcc", and the absence of the attribute MUST be treated as if it had been set to "bcc".

When creating a recipient-history list, servers use the "bcc" values to route the request, and they must treat "bcc" marked URIs in one of two ways. Either the server removes all "bcc" marked URIs from the recipient-history lists, which lets it send the same list to every recipient but leaves blind recipients unaware that they were blind copies. Or the server preserves the "bcc" marked URI that identifies the recipient itself, and removes the remaining ones, so each recipient receives a different list and blind recipients are explicitly informed.

The new 'anonymize' attribute can be included in an entry element. If set to "true", it asks the server not to disclose the URI in the list sent to the recipient, but to replace it with an anonymous one. Servers may use such URIs for routing, but MUST convert them to the SIP URI "sip:anonymous@anonymous.invalid" in recipient-history lists. The default value of the attribute is "false". The anonymize attribute overlaps with the "bcc" value in appearance but not in effect: a "bcc" URI is removed entirely and recipients do not notice that extra blind copies exist, while an anonymized URI is replaced by an anonymous one, so recipients notice that there were more recipients without learning who they are. The new 'count' attribute gives the number of equal URIs, and its default value is "1". Where several URIs are anonymized, the server can group them into a single anonymous URI within its copy control level and give the count of anonymized URIs. Processing of URIs tagged "bcc" has higher precedence over the anonymize attribute, so if the copyControl of a URI is "bcc" the server MUST remove that URI from the recipient-history list and the anonymize attribute is ignored.

Duplicate URI entries in a resource list are considered an error, since there is no reasonable use for them. A server should not send duplicated copies of the same request to the same intended recipient, so it should send at most a single copy. For each set of duplicated entries, the server MUST select the highest precedence value of copyControl, and the order of precedence is "to", "cc" and "bcc".
sections.plainLanguage: Each address carries a label: to, cc or bcc. An address without a label counts as bcc. The server hides bcc addresses from the list it passes on. A separate anonymize flag hides the name but keeps the count visible, so recipients know that others were included.

sections.title: The XML Schema
sections.content:
The extension is defined as an XML schema with the target namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:copycontrol, which imports the resource lists namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:resource-lists, and with qualified element forms and unqualified attribute forms. The schema documents itself as adding the copyControl, anonymize and count attributes to URIs included in a resource list.

The copyControl attribute is a string restricted to an enumeration of three values: "to", "cc" and "bcc". The anonymize attribute is of the boolean type with a default of "false", and the count attribute is of the non-negative integer type with a default of "1". Implementations according to this specification MUST support this XML schema, and the copyControl, anonymize and count attributes SHOULD be included as modifiers of any of the child elements included in the list element of a resource list, such as the entry or external elements.
sections.plainLanguage: The attributes are defined in a small XML schema under their own namespace, so a receiving system can tell them apart from ordinary resource list attributes. The count attribute is a whole number that cannot be negative.

sections.title: A Recipient List and Its Recipient-History List
sections.content:
The RFC's first example is the recipient list a User Agent Client sends to the URI-list server, carried in the F2 flow of Figure 1. It is a flat list in the resource list data format, where each entry states the copy control of that resource, and some entries are also marked with the anonymize attribute to indicate that their URIs should not be disclosed. The last two entries are marked with a copyControl of "bcc", which indicates that the server should remove them from the recipient-history list.

On receipt, the server creates a SIP request for each URI in the recipient list, seven in the example, and builds a recipient-history list for each. It first copies all the URIs marked "to" or "cc" that do not carry the anonymize attribute. Then the URIs marked "to" with anonymize set to "true" are replaced with the SIP anonymous URI, keeping the original copyControl value of "to" and adding a count attribute with the number of anonymous entries in the group, which is "2" in the example. The server then does the same for the URIs marked "cc" with anonymize set to "true", adding a count of "1". Last, it removes all the URIs marked "bcc". The resulting list, shown in the RFC, holds four entries: one visible "to" address, one anonymous "to" entry with count 2, one visible "cc" address and one anonymous "cc" entry with count 1.
sections.plainLanguage: In the worked example the sender lists seven addresses. What each recipient actually receives is a four-entry list: two visible names and two anonymous entries that say how many hidden addresses they stand for.

sections.title: Carrying URI Lists in SIP
sections.content:
A SIP User Agent Client that composes a request can include a URI list with these extensions to indicate the list of intended recipients. As specified in RFC 5363, the User Agent adds a Content-Disposition header field set to the value 'recipient-list'. A body whose Content-Disposition type is 'recipient-list' contains the intended recipients of the request, which is what this document calls a recipient list. The entry element in the URI list may also include the copyControl and anonymize attributes.

To be able to inform intended recipients of who else is receiving a copy, the RFC defines a new mail disposition type for the Content-Disposition header field of a SIP request. The value is 'recipient-list-history', and a body with that disposition type contains a URI list with the visible recipients of the request, including anonymized ones. The entry element in that list may also include the copyControl and count attributes.

On sending a request that contains a recipient-history list, if the intended recipient does not support this specification the request should not fail. To ensure successful receipt of requests that include 'recipient-list-history' bodies, User Agents that build such requests SHOULD add a "handling" parameter set to "optional". Otherwise the request could fail and never be received. A further limitation is that even though message body handling in SIP mandates support for multipart bodies, legacy recipients may not support them. If the request the relay sends needs to contain another body, such as a MESSAGE request carrying a message, the relay cannot use this extension, because the recipient would not be able to process a multipart body with the original body plus the recipient-list-history body.
sections.plainLanguage: The two lists travel as SIP message bodies with different labels: one says who should get the request, the other says who did. The server adds a handling parameter so that a recipient that does not understand the second list still accepts the request.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations of this specification MUST follow the security-related rules of RFC 5363, which include opt-in lists and mandatory authentication and authorization of clients. User Agent Clients SHOULD NOT hand SIP requests containing URI-list services to unauthenticated and untrusted parties, to avoid man-in-the-middle attacks and to avoid acquiring URI lists for use in spam attacks.

URI lists may contain private information such as SIP URIs, so it is not desirable that these lists are known by third parties. Eavesdroppers can watch URI lists in SIP requests unless the SIP message is sent over a secured channel using a mechanism such as Transport Layer Security, or unless the URI-list body itself is encrypted with, for example, S/MIME. It is therefore RECOMMENDED that URI-list bodies are encrypted with S/MIME or that the SIP request is encrypted with TLS or another suitable encryption mechanism.

The list does not indicate the actual participants in the session, only the URIs invited and that might accept the request. It does not assert that these parties exist, that they are reachable, or that they accepted the invitation, and no inference about billing should be drawn from it. It is subject to spoofing by loading the list with falsified content.

The "bcc" copy control is used to send requests without revealing the URIs of other recipients, and mishandling it can reveal confidential information, which could eventually lead to security problems through knowledge of even the existence of a particular URI. With the first method, where the "bcc" tagged URIs are removed from the recipient-history list, blind recipients have no explicit indication that they were sent a blind copy, except in so far as their URI does not appear in the list, so one of them could reply to all the shown recipients and accidentally reveal that the message went to the blind recipient. With the second method, the blind recipient's address appears in the recipient-history list of a separate copy of the list, so even if a separate message is sent to each blind recipient with only that individual's URI, implementations still need to process replies carefully so as not to reveal the blind recipient to others.
sections.plainLanguage: The list of addresses is private, so it should travel encrypted. A blind copy must stay blind, which means a recipient who cannot see their own address in the list should not be able to reply to everyone, or the hidden recipients would be exposed.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA has made three registrations on behalf of this document. The first is a new disposition type: the value 'recipient-list-history' is registered in the IANA registry of Mail Content Disposition Values, with the description that the body contains a list of URIs indicating the recipients of the request, and this document as the reference.

The second is a new XML namespace, registered in the IANA XML registry following the guidelines of RFC 3688. The URI for the namespace is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:copycontrol, and the registrant contact is the IETF SIPPING working group together with the named author. The third is a new XML schema, also registered in the IANA XML registry following the procedures of RFC 3688, with the URI urn:ietf:params:xml:schema:copycontrol and the same registrant contact. The XML for the schema is the sole content of Section 5 of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: The document asks IANA for three reservations: a new body label, a new XML namespace for the attributes and a new XML schema.
